questions.prompt: Put these four stages of Microsoft's own framing of "how Data Factory works" in the correct order, per Lesson 1.
items: Connect & collect — reach into on-premises and cloud sources alike, moving raw data into one centralized store
Transform & enrich — process the collected data, visually with mapping data flows or by calling out to a compute service
CI/CD & publish — develop and test pipelines like real code, then load business-ready data into a destination
Monitor — track every pipeline run's success and failure, with built-in alerts and logging
questions.explain: Lesson 1 breaks nearly everything a data engineer does with Data Factory into these four stages, in this order: collect the raw data first, transform and enrich it, publish the finished, tested result, and then monitor it in production. Every later chapter in this course maps onto one of these four stages.

questions.prompt: A company has been running Azure Data Factory in production for two years, with dozens of stable, working hybrid pipelines. Per Lesson 3's decision guide, what's the right call?
options: Stay on ADF — Microsoft has kept its feature set stable rather than actively growing it, but it isn't going away, and migrating working pipelines for its own sake rarely pays off
Migrate everything to Fabric Data Factory immediately, since it's the newer platform
Switch back to SSIS, since it's the most mature of the three tools
Rebuild every pipeline using only mapping data flows, since those are Spark-powered
questions.explain: Lesson 3's practical decision guide is explicit: an existing, stable hybrid pipeline already built in ADF should stay on ADF. "Fabric is newer" isn't, by itself, a good enough reason to migrate dozens of working production pipelines — Fabric is where Microsoft recommends starting a brand-new, cloud-native project with no legacy dependency, which this scenario isn't.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a new data factory's name must be ________ unique across all of Azure, not just within your own subscription.
questions.explain: Lesson 4 is specific about this: a data factory's name is checked against every Azure customer's data factories, not just your own. If your first choice is taken, Microsoft's own convention is to try something like <yourname>ADFTutorialDataFactory instead.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a linked service in Azure Data Factory?
options: A connection definition — like a connection string — telling Data Factory how to reach a specific data store or compute resource
A named pointer to the specific table, file, or folder that an activity actually reads from or writes to
A single processing step, like copying data or running a query
The compute environment that actually executes an activity
A logical grouping of activities that together perform one unit of work
A reusable expression, starting with @, evaluated at pipeline runtime
questions.explain: A linked service is specifically the connection definition — how to reach a data store or compute resource. You create one once per data store and reuse it across as many datasets and pipelines as you need, rather than recreating the connection every time.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a dataset, not a linked service — exactly the point of confusion Lesson 6 calls out directly. The linked service defines how to connect; the dataset defines which specific data, inside that connection, you actually mean. Mixing the two up is the single most common early mistake with this pair of concepts.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Azure Blob Storage linked service authentication, per Lesson 7.
options: A system-assigned managed identity means there's no credential to store, rotate, or ever let leak at all
Account key authentication grants full access to the entire storage account, not just one container
Anonymous authentication is the recommended default for a production pipeline
A shared access signature (SAS) is more scoped and time-limited than a full account key
Testing the connection is unnecessary once the configuration form itself validates with no errors
questions.explain: A managed identity eliminates stored credentials entirely. An account key, by contrast, grants full access to the whole storage account — a real risk beyond a learning environment. A SAS is deliberately narrower and time-limited. Anonymous access is for public, unauthenticated containers only, essentially never production. And Test connection catches real problems — a typo, a firewall rule, a permission that hasn't propagated — that simple form validation never checks.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lesson 6 to what it actually is.
right: The connector-specific connection details inside a linked service's JSON
Defines how to connect to a specific data store or compute resource
The integration runtime setting controlling which compute executes a connection
A named view pointing to the specific table, file, or folder inside a connection
questions.explain: A linked service defines how to connect. A dataset is a named view of the specific data inside that connection. typeProperties holds the connector-specific details — a connection string, a server name — inside the linked service's JSON. connectVia names which integration runtime actually executes that connection, defaulting to the Azure Integration Runtime if omitted.

questions.prompt: A Copy activity has no explicit mapping configured on its Mapping tab. On the next run, the source table has gained a new column that didn't exist before. What happens?
options: The new column flows through automatically to the sink, by name — default mapping supports schema drift, with no pipeline change required
The pipeline fails immediately, because the sink's schema no longer matches the source exactly
The new column is silently dropped, and only the originally-seen columns copy through
The Copy activity requires someone to manually re-run Import schemas before it will recognize the new column
questions.explain: With no mapping configured, the Copy activity maps source to sink by column name by default — and that default behavior genuinely supports schema drift. Whatever the source actually returns on a given run, including a brand-new column, flows through with no pipeline change required. This is exactly why explicit mapping (which doesn't embrace drift the same way) is a deliberate trade-off, not a strict upgrade.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Lookup activity's real limits, per Lesson 14.
options: It returns a maximum of 5,000 rows
Its output is capped at 4 MB, and it fails outright if that's exceeded
It has a maximum duration of 24 hours before timing out
A query or stored procedure used for a lookup can return more than one result set, and the activity simply uses the first one
Setting firstRowOnly to false returns every matching row, as a value array, along with a count
questions.explain: The Lookup activity caps out at 5,000 rows, 4 MB of output, and a 24-hour duration. firstRowOnly: false switches it from returning a single firstRow to returning every matching row in a value array with a count — exactly the shape a ForEach activity expects. A query or procedure returning more than one result set isn't quietly handled by using the first one — the activity fails outright, since a lookup query must return exactly one result set.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the Stored Procedure activity can't be used to return a value back to the pipeline, because it doesn't support ________ parameters — a Lookup activity (or a Script activity) is needed instead.
questions.explain: The Stored Procedure activity is a one-way call: it invokes a procedure and supplies input values, but genuinely doesn't support output parameters. A stored procedure that needs to hand a value back to the pipeline needs the Lookup activity (or a Script activity), not the Stored Procedure activity.

questions.prompt: In Lesson 16's end-to-end pipeline, the Copy activity connects to the Stored Procedure activity with a Succeeded dependency condition, and separately to a Fail activity with a Failed dependency condition. If the Copy activity itself fails, what happens?
options: Only the Fail activity runs — the Stored Procedure activity is never triggered, since its Succeeded condition wasn't met
Both the Stored Procedure and Fail activities run, since a dependency condition doesn't actually control whether an activity executes
The Stored Procedure activity still runs anyway, because dependency conditions only affect the pipeline's final reported status, not which activities execute
The pipeline automatically retries the Copy activity before either dependency condition is ever evaluated
questions.explain: Every connection between two activities carries a dependency condition — Succeeded, Failed, Skipped, or Completed — that genuinely controls whether the downstream activity runs at all. A Copy failure means the Succeeded condition feeding Stored Procedure was never met, so that activity doesn't run; only the Failed-conditioned Fail activity fires, stopping the pipeline loudly with a clear message instead of silently doing nothing.

questions.prompt: A pipeline needs to track, mid-run, whether an earlier validation step has passed yet, so a later If Condition can check it. Per Lesson 17, which should this be, and why?
options: A variable — because its value needs to change while the pipeline is actually running, which a parameter genuinely can't do
A parameter — because it controls pipeline behavior from outside the run
Either works identically, since parameters can also be modified mid-run with the Set Variable activity
A SecureString parameter, so the validation flag stays hidden from the If Condition's own expression
questions.explain: Lesson 17's one-sentence distinction settles this directly: parameters are external, set once, from outside a pipeline; variables are internal and mutable, changed from inside a pipeline as it runs, using the Set Variable activity. Tracking whether a validation step has passed yet is exactly the kind of in-flight state a variable exists for — a parameter can't be modified mid-run at all.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the ForEach activity, per Lesson 19.
options: A ForEach activity can't directly contain another ForEach or an Until activity
isSequential: false, the default, runs iterations in parallel, up to batchCount
batchCount can be set as high as 500 for a sufficiently large array
@item() inside a nested activity references whatever value the current iteration is actually processing
Setting a pipeline variable inside a parallel ForEach is always perfectly safe, since each iteration gets its own private copy
questions.explain: ForEach genuinely can't nest another ForEach or Until directly — the documented workaround is an Execute Pipeline activity containing the inner loop. Parallel is the default, bounded by batchCount, which maxes out at 50, not 500. @item() is exactly how a nested activity references the current iteration's value. And variables are scoped to the entire pipeline, not per-iteration — they are explicitly not thread-safe, so writing to one inside a parallel ForEach is a real risk, not a safe default.

questions.prompt: Inside an Until activity's child activities, one child activity fails on a given pass through the loop. What happens to the Until activity as a whole?
options: It keeps looping, running the child activities again, until the expression evaluates true or the timeout is reached
It immediately fails and stops looping the moment any child activity fails
It skips that pass's failed activity and treats the loop's own expression as automatically true
It pauses indefinitely until someone manually resumes the pipeline
questions.explain: Lesson 20 states this real behavior explicitly: if a child activity inside an Until loop fails, the Until activity doesn't stop — it keeps looping until the expression is true or the timeout is reached. That's precisely why a sensible, explicit timeout matters: without one, a condition that never becomes true, combined with a child activity that keeps failing, would otherwise consume resources for up to the 7-day default.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: wrapping an expression in @{...} inside a string, like "Answer is: @{pipeline().parameters.myNumber}", forces the result into a string — this is called string ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 22 names this pattern directly: @{...} wrapped inside a string is string interpolation, forcing the enclosed expression's result into a string — useful the moment you're building a dynamic file name or message rather than passing a typed value through untouched.

questions.prompt: A data flow source has "Allow schema drift" turned on, but "Infer drifted column types" turned off. A newly arrived column that wasn't in the defined schema flows through. What type does Data Factory assign it?
options: string, by default
Whatever type best matches the sampled values, inferred automatically regardless of the setting
The data flow fails outright, since every column must have an inferred type
int, since an untyped drifted column defaults to numeric
questions.explain: Lesson 25 is explicit about this pairing: "Allow schema drift" lets new columns flow through at all, while "Infer drifted column types" controls whether Data Factory actually detects a real type for them. With inference turned off, a drifted column simply defaults to string rather than failing or guessing a numeric type.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Aggregate transformation, per Lesson 27.
options: A column left out of both the group-by clause and every aggregate expression doesn't flow through to the output at all
Aggregate behaves like a SQL SELECT with a GROUP BY, not like a row-preserving transformation
Deduplication can be done by grouping on the columns that define a duplicate, then applying first() or last() to every other column
count() inside the same aggregation can report how many duplicate rows existed before they were collapsed
An unlisted column is automatically kept using its first row's value, with no extra configuration needed
questions.explain: Any column not in the group-by clause or an aggregate expression genuinely vanishes from the output — Aggregate behaves exactly like a SQL GROUP BY, not a row-preserving step. That's also the mechanism behind deduplication: group on what defines a duplicate, then use first()/last() (via a column pattern) on everything else, with count() reporting how many rows collapsed into one. Nothing is kept automatically — every surviving column has to be aggregated or grouped on explicitly.

questions.prompt: Match each mapping data flow transformation to what it actually does.
right: Routes each row to the first matching stream, CASE-statement style
Keeps only rows matching a boolean expression, like a WHERE clause
Creates new columns or overwrites existing ones, using an expression
Renames, drops, or reorders columns, without changing any row's actual values
questions.explain: Filter is a visual WHERE clause — it keeps or drops entire rows. Select reshapes only the column list: rename, drop, reorder, with row values untouched. Derived Column creates or overwrites column values via an expression. Conditional Split routes each row to the first matching stream (or a default), the visual equivalent of a CASE decision structure.

questions.prompt: A data flow's monitoring view shows cluster start-up at 40 seconds, source read at 12 seconds, transformation at 6 minutes, and sink write at 15 seconds. Per Lesson 29, where should tuning effort go first?
options: The transformation stage, since it's by far the largest number in the monitoring view
Cluster start-up, since that's always the first place to optimize regardless of its actual duration
Sink write, since writing to a destination is typically assumed to be the slowest stage
All four stages equally, splitting the optimization effort evenly across each one
questions.explain: Lesson 29's rule is direct: find the largest number in the monitoring view first — that's where tuning effort actually pays off, not wherever intuition points. At 6 minutes against three stages each under a minute, the transformation stage is overwhelmingly the real bottleneck here, and that's exactly where repartitioning or a larger integration runtime should be considered first.

questions.prompt: What is the primary characteristic that distinguishes a tumbling window trigger from a Schedule trigger?
options: It retains state across fixed-size, non-overlapping, contiguous windows, and supports backfill plus automatic retry
It can start multiple different pipelines at once, the same way a Schedule trigger can
It fires in response to a file arriving in Blob Storage, rather than on any time-based interval
It requires no recurrence or interval to be configured at all
It is the only one of the two trigger types that supports a wall-clock schedule
It has no upper limit on how many windows can run concurrently
questions.explain: A tumbling window trigger's defining feature is retaining state across gap-free, non-overlapping windows — which is exactly what unlocks automatic backfill of missed windows and a built-in retryPolicy, neither of which a Schedule trigger supports at all.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes exactly the opposite of reality. A Schedule trigger has a many-to-many relationship with pipelines — it can start several pipelines, and a pipeline can have several triggers. A tumbling window trigger has a strict one-to-one relationship with a single pipeline. Swapping these two around is a common point of confusion between the two trigger types.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement comparing a tumbling window trigger to a Schedule trigger, per Lesson 31.
options: Only a tumbling window trigger supports backfill — automatically running every missed window between a past start time and now
A tumbling window trigger's retryPolicy automatically retries a failed pipeline run using the same input parameters
A Schedule trigger's run state reflects whether its pipeline actually succeeded or failed, the same way a tumbling window trigger's does
maxConcurrency on a tumbling window trigger can be set anywhere from 1 to 50
A Schedule trigger can only ever be wired to exactly one pipeline, just like a tumbling window trigger
questions.explain: Backfill, automatic retry, and a maxConcurrency range of 1-50 are all real tumbling window trigger features with no Schedule trigger equivalent. A Schedule trigger is genuinely "fire and forget" — it succeeds once started, regardless of whether the pipeline itself later fails, unlike a tumbling window trigger's run state. And a Schedule trigger has a many-to-many relationship with pipelines, the opposite of a tumbling window trigger's strict one-to-one relationship.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a tumbling window trigger can depend on up to ________ other triggers.
questions.explain: Lesson 33 states this limit directly: a tumbling window trigger can depend on up to five other triggers, each with its own offset and size, letting a real dependency chain express something like "don't start today's aggregation until yesterday's ingestion actually finished."

questions.prompt: A Copy activity's source linked service points to a self-hosted integration runtime, while its sink linked service uses the default Azure Integration Runtime. Which integration runtime actually executes this Copy activity?
options: The self-hosted integration runtime — if either the source or sink linked service points to one, the whole copy runs on it, with no mixing of runtimes
The Azure Integration Runtime, since it's the more broadly capable, fully managed option
Both run simultaneously, with the two results merged together afterward
The copy fails outright, because a source and sink can't reference two different integration runtime types
questions.explain: Lesson 12 and Lesson 34 are both explicit about this: for a Copy activity, if either the source or sink linked service points to a self-hosted integration runtime, the entire copy runs on that self-hosted runtime. There's no mixing — you can't run half the copy on one runtime and half on another.

questions.prompt: Match each integration runtime type to the job it's actually built for.
right: A managed cluster of Azure VMs, purpose-built to run existing SSIS packages
Software installed on your own network, bridging Data Factory to on-premises or private-network data
Fully managed, serverless compute for cloud-to-cloud data movement, activity dispatch, and data flows
questions.explain: The Azure IR is fully managed and serverless, handling cloud-to-cloud work with nothing to provision. The self-hosted IR is software you install yourself, specifically to bridge the gap the Azure IR can't cross — a private network or on-premises system. The Azure-SSIS IR is a managed VM cluster with one specific job: natively running existing SSIS packages.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a self-hosted integration runtime only ever needs ________ access on port 443 — no inbound firewall rule is required at all.
questions.explain: Lesson 37 makes this the central, reassuring fact for any security review: every connection a self-hosted IR makes is outbound, initiated by the IR machine itself, on port 443. Nobody has to open an inbound port for Azure to reach into the network — standard corporate firewalls already allow outbound HTTPS by default.

questions.code:
CopyActivity --Upon Failure--> ErrorHandler
(no Upon Success path is defined from CopyActivity at all)
questions.prompt: A pipeline connects CopyActivity's Upon Failure path to ErrorHandler, but defines no Upon Success path from CopyActivity at all. If CopyActivity fails and ErrorHandler then succeeds, what does the overall pipeline status show?
options: Succeeded — Data Factory evaluates only leaf activities to decide overall status, and ErrorHandler, the leaf here, succeeded
Failed — any activity failing anywhere in the pipeline always fails the whole run
Succeeded, but only if an Upon Skip path was also explicitly defined somewhere
The pipeline's status is left blank, since the two paths conflict with each other
questions.explain: This is Lesson 40's Try-Catch pattern exactly: defining only an Upon Failure path doesn't make the overall pipeline "fail." Data Factory evaluates only leaf activities — the ones with nothing downstream — to decide overall success. Since ErrorHandler is the leaf activity here and it succeeded, the pipeline reports Succeeded even though CopyActivity itself failed.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about an activity's retry policy block, per Lesson 39.
options: The default number of retries is 0 — you have to opt in explicitly
retryIntervalInSeconds controls the delay between retry attempts
The default timeout for an activity is 12 hours
secureOutput: true means the activity's output isn't logged for monitoring
Retry policies and alerts solve the exact same problem, so configuring both is redundant
questions.explain: An activity's policy block defaults to zero retries, a 30-second retryIntervalInSeconds between attempts, and a 12-hour timeout — all opt-in behaviors. secureOutput: true keeps sensitive output out of monitoring logs. Retry policies and alerts are deliberately two different tools: a retry quietly absorbs a transient failure before anyone needs to know, while an alert exists specifically for failures a retry couldn't fix — configuring both covers two genuinely different problems, not one.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Data Factory only stores pipeline run history in the Monitor hub for ________ days, which is exactly why routing diagnostics to Log Analytics matters for any factory you care about long-term.
questions.explain: Lesson 41 calls this out as a fact that catches people off guard: 45 days of retention in the Monitor hub, genuinely built for recent troubleshooting rather than a permanent audit trail. Answering a question like "how has this pipeline's failure rate trended over six months" requires a diagnostic setting streaming to Log Analytics instead.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of debugging a failed pipeline run in the correct order, per Lesson 38.
items: Notice the pipeline's overall status shows Failed in the Monitor hub's pipeline runs list
Click into that pipeline run to open its activity runs, to see which specific activity actually broke
Click the error icon on the failed activity and read its failure type and exception message
Once the underlying problem is fixed, use Rerun from failed activity to avoid redoing already-succeeded work
questions.explain: A pipeline-level Failed status only tells you that something broke, not which activity. The real debugging flow drills from the pipeline runs list into that run's activity runs, reads the actual error (the failure type field is worth reading first), fixes the underlying cause, and then rerun from the failed activity specifically — skipping everything upstream that already succeeded, rather than restarting the entire pipeline from scratch.

questions.prompt: A Dataflow Gen2 loads data into a Fabric Lakehouse table. A data scientist then attaches a Spark notebook directly to that same table, with no connector and no export step. Why does this work?
options: Because OneLake stores the table in the open Delta Parquet format, so any compatible engine — including Spark — can read the exact same bytes directly
Because Fabric automatically creates a hidden copy of the table for every workload that needs it
Because Dataflow Gen2 and Spark notebooks always run on the same underlying compute cluster
Because Lakehouse tables are exempt from needing any defined schema at all
questions.explain: Lesson 45's "one copy of data" claim is technically grounded in the storage format itself: OneLake stores tables as Delta Parquet, an open, standard format any compatible engine can read natively, with no custom connector required. A Spark notebook, a T-SQL query, and a Power BI Direct Lake report can all read the exact same physical bytes — not four separate copies.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement comparing Dataflow Gen2 to classic mapping data flows, per Lesson 43.
options: Dataflow Gen2 is built on Power Query (M), not Apache Spark
Dataflow Gen2 has no separate debug mode — it's always interactive
Dataflow Gen2 can write to Fabric-native destinations, like Lakehouse Tables, that classic mapping data flows never supported
Mapping data flows and Dataflow Gen2 use the exact same underlying engine, just with a different user interface
A heavy, large-scale join-and-aggregate transformation across huge datasets still plays to Spark's real strengths
questions.explain: Dataflow Gen2's engine is genuinely Power Query (M), not Spark — a deliberate, different choice from mapping data flows, not a rename. It's always interactive, with no separate debug-mode toggle to turn on first. It supports destinations, including Fabric-native Lakehouse Tables and Warehouse, that classic mapping data flows never had as options. And for heavy, large-scale transformation, Spark (mapping data flows, or Fabric's own Spark notebooks) genuinely remains the better fit — the two engines aren't the same thing wearing different UI.

questions.prompt: Match each classic Azure Data Factory concept to its Fabric Data Factory equivalent, per Lessons 43-44.
questions.explain: Fabric drops the separate dataset object entirely — connection properties are defined inline, through Connections. Mapping data flows become Dataflow Gen2, the same visual idea on a different (Power Query) engine. There's no separate publish step — Save stores your work, Run executes it immediately. And duplicating a pipeline, which classic ADF did through an ARM template export/import round trip, becomes Fabric's one-click Save As.

questions.prompt: A company runs dozens of real SSIS packages through ADF's Azure-SSIS integration runtime. Per Lesson 46, what does this mean for migrating those specific pipelines to Fabric right now?
options: There's currently no direct Fabric equivalent for Azure-SSIS — those pipelines should stay on classic ADF for now
They migrate automatically through the built-in upgrade experience, with no changes needed
They should be rebuilt using a single, unified Databricks activity
Fabric's On-premises Data Gateway replaces Azure-SSIS directly, one for one
questions.explain: Lesson 46's honest list is direct about this: the Azure-SSIS integration runtime is still "to be determined" in Fabric as of this course. Pipelines genuinely dependent on running real SSIS packages have no migration path today — the right call is keeping them on classic ADF, not forcing a rebuild onto a feature gap that doesn't exist yet.

questions.prompt: What does a system-assigned managed identity actually eliminate for a data factory's linked services?
options: The need to ever store, rotate, or let leak a separate credential, for any resource that grants that identity access directly
The need to configure any linked service at all
The need for role-based access control on any target resource
The need to use Azure Key Vault for any secret, under any circumstance
The need for a self-hosted integration runtime when connecting to on-premises data
The requirement that a data factory have only one linked service per connector type
questions.explain: A managed identity gives Data Factory its own identity in Microsoft Entra ID. Other Azure services can grant that identity access directly, so there's no credential — no connection string, key, or password — sitting in the linked service to store, rotate, or leak at all.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D sounds related, since both managed identities and Key Vault reduce how secrets are handled, but they solve different problems. A managed identity removes the need for a stored credential only on resources that support identity-based access directly. Key Vault is still the right place for a genuine secret a linked service needs to hold, like an on-premises SQL Server connection string — one doesn't make the other unnecessary.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Git integration in Data Factory, per Lesson 50.
options: Publish is only available from the collaboration branch — never directly from a feature branch
Publishing writes generated ARM templates to a separate branch, adf_publish by default
A linked service still using a raw, non-Key-Vault-backed password publishes immediately, bypassing the Git workflow for that one resource
The collaboration branch is always a live, up-to-date reflection of what's actually running in the factory
Feature branches require Data Factory Contributor permissions just to save work to them
questions.explain: Publish genuinely only works from the collaboration branch, writing ARM templates to adf_publish. A raw, non-Key-Vault-backed secret bypasses the Git workflow entirely and publishes the moment it's saved — a deliberate exception, since Data Factory never writes secrets into Git. But the collaboration branch is never guaranteed to match what's actually live — it has to be published, manually or via automation, to take effect. And saving to a feature branch only needs Git repo write access, not Data Factory Contributor permissions — that's exactly what makes the "can edit, can't publish" pattern work.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Data Factory doesn't support publishing only some of your changes — every publish pushes everything currently in the collaboration branch. This is informally the no-________ rule.
questions.explain: Lesson 51 states this directly: publishing means everything in the collaboration branch, every time, because entities genuinely depend on each other — triggers depend on pipelines, pipelines depend on datasets — and a partial publish risks leaving the factory inconsistent. A narrow, urgent fix goes through a dedicated hotfix process instead, not selective publishing.

questions.code:
Deployment Task:
  Action: Create or update resource group
  Mode: Complete
  Template: ARMTemplateForFactory.json
questions.prompt: A release pipeline's ARM Template Deployment task is set to deployment mode Complete instead of Incremental, and the new template happens to be missing a linked service that currently exists in the target resource group. What happens on deployment?
options: The existing linked service gets deleted, since Complete mode removes any resource not present in the new template
The deployment simply leaves that linked service untouched, exactly as Incremental mode would
The deployment fails outright with a validation error before anything changes
The missing linked service is automatically recreated from the last known ARM template
questions.explain: Lesson 52 is direct about why Incremental, not Complete, is the right default: in Complete mode, any resource that exists in the resource group but isn't present in the new template gets deleted. A linked service simply missing from this particular deployment's template — not something anyone intended to remove — would be destroyed, which is exactly the real risk Incremental mode avoids by only adding and updating.

questions.prompt: Match each piece of Northwind's stakeholder ask to the technical course concept that actually satisfies it, per Lesson 53.
left: "Cleaned up and totaled by region and category"
"Every morning before 8 AM, on its own"
"No passwords sitting around in plain text"
right: Mapping data flow: filter, aggregate, join
questions.explain: Lesson 53's translation table maps each plain-language requirement to a real technical piece: an on-premises source needs the self-hosted integration runtime bridge; "cleaned up and totaled" is a mapping data flow's filter, join, and aggregate; unattended scheduling needs a Schedule trigger plus real error handling; and no exposed passwords means managed identity and Key Vault throughout. None of the four was handed over as "use activity X" — translating business language into architecture is the actual skill this lesson is teaching.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 56's mapping data flow in the correct order.
items: Filter out cancelled orders and internal test transactions before any other transformation runs
Join in Region from the Store dimension table
Join in Category from the Product dimension table
Aggregate, grouping by Region and Category, summing OrderAmount into TotalSales
Write the result to the curated Azure SQL Database table, with the sink's Update method set to Overwrite
questions.explain: Filtering first means every downstream step processes less data, and a cancelled order can never inflate a regional total. The two joins have to happen before the aggregate, since you can't group by a Region or Category column that doesn't exist on the row yet. Only once every row carries both columns does the Aggregate produce the stakeholder's actual ask, and Overwrite on the sink ensures a second same-day run replaces yesterday's totals cleanly instead of duplicating rows.

questions.prompt: Northwind's capstone pipeline uses a retry policy, a Try-Catch-Proceed pattern, and a scoped alert — three separate error-handling layers, not just one. Per Lesson 55, why?
options: Each layer only escalates to the next when the previous one genuinely couldn't handle the problem — a retry absorbs brief blips silently, Try-Catch-Proceed logs sustained failures without blocking the run, and the alert wakes a human only as the deliberate last resort
Because a single retry policy alone is technically incapable of ever catching any failure at all
Because Data Factory requires at least three separate error-handling mechanisms on every production pipeline
Because Try-Catch-Proceed and the alert both only function if a retry policy is also present on the same activity
questions.explain: Lesson 55 lays this out as a deliberate escalation design, not redundancy: most real 3 AM problems are transient, and the retry policy silently absorbs those with zero human involvement. A sustained failure that survives all retries gets logged by Try-Catch-Proceed, leaving an audit trail without erroring the whole run. Only a failure serious enough that logging genuinely isn't sufficient — Northwind losing an entire night's sales data — reaches the alert that actually pages someone. Each layer exists specifically for what the layer before it couldn't fix.

questions.prompt: Lesson 54's Copy activity lands yesterday's raw sales data as Parquet in the ADLS Gen2 raw zone, not CSV. Why Parquet specifically?
options: It's columnar with schema embedded in the file itself, and it's the same format OneLake uses natively — letting the later mapping data flow read only the columns it actually needs
Parquet is a hard requirement of the Copy activity's auto-create-table feature for any SQL sink
A self-hosted integration runtime is physically unable to read or write CSV files
Parquet files don't require any defined schema at all, unlike a CSV file
questions.explain: Lesson 54 gives three concrete reasons: Parquet's columnar layout lets the Lesson 56 data flow read just the handful of columns its aggregation needs, its schema travels embedded in the file so nothing downstream has to guess it separately, and it's the same format Fabric's OneLake uses natively, useful if Northwind's platform ever grows in that direction. None of that is about the sink type or the integration runtime, and Parquet's embedded schema is actually the opposite of schema-less.
